domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: Merchants cannot tell AI shopping agents from malicious bots, nor attribute agent-driven sales
affected_user: Online retailers and small Shopify/DTC merchants, plus their fraud/analytics staff
job_to_be_done: Admit legitimate shopping agents to product pages and checkout while blocking scrapers and card-testing bots, and measure which orders came from agents
current_process: Generic bot management (Cloudflare, proof-of-work challenges like Anubis, WAF rules) tuned for human-vs-bot; web analytics keyed on referrer; manual decisions about whether to let agents into checkout (QVC allows, Tapestry and Amazon block)
what_fails: Agent traffic and scraper traffic look alike: operators report bots passing difficulty-6 proof-of-work challenges from residential IPs; merchants cannot connect agent traffic to completed orders; integrations with agent checkouts (OpenAI Instant Checkout) were error-prone, lacked sales-tax handling, and listed only about 30 Shopify merchants before OpenAI retreated to on-site checkout in March 2026
failure_frequency: Continuous. PYMNTS/Visa survey: only 23% of merchants can identify both AI-driven traffic and purchases; 21% see agent traffic but cannot link it to orders. Adobe: AI-referred US retail traffic +393% YoY in Q1 2026. BCG: external agent referrals <1% of EU brand visits late 2025, ~5% expected by end 2026
cost_of_failure: Unknown in dollars. Indirect: lost attribution for a channel Adobe says converts 42% better than non-AI traffic (March 2026); OpenAI's in-chat checkout reportedly charged merchants 4% per sale (press reports, never published by OpenAI); bandwidth and security spend on bot filtering
existing_workaround: Block all non-human traffic (losing agent buyers), or allow everything and absorb scraping/card-testing; rely on self-reported platform stats (Shopify figures are unaudited); keep checkout on-site and let agents only discover
who_pays_today: Merchants (bot-management SaaS, fraud tooling, developer time for ACP/AP2 integrations); payment networks building protocols (Visa Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard, Stripe Shared Payment Tokens at $0.15/token issued)

sources.note: Visa-sponsored survey: 23% of merchants can identify both AI traffic and purchases; 21% see traffic but cannot link to orders
Adobe Digital Insights: AI-referred retail traffic +393% YoY Q1 2026, converts 42% better
Agent referrals <1% of visits late 2025, could reach ~5% by end 2026; referral counts understate influence
Retailers split: QVC allows agent checkout, Tapestry and Amazon block outside agents

Reported 4% merchant fee on Instant Checkout orders; OpenAI never published the rate
hgweb operator says bots still pass difficulty-6 challenge; contributor says bot IPs are residential, likely proxy networks
ACP issue: 'merchant has no stored agent identity'
ACP OpenAPI rejects six fields its own JSON schema declares; several similar schema-mismatch issues

firsthand_evidence: An operator of two Mercurial hosting sites (Oct 17, 2026) reported that even with Anubis at a difficulty-6 proof-of-work challenge, many bots still get through, and he had to re-enable password authentication on top; a project contributor replied that the bot IPs appear residential, likely a proxy network or compromised devices. ACP developers filed issues that the spec's OpenAPI rejects fields its own schema declares and that merchants have no stored agent identity.
key_unknowns: No Reddit/Shopify-forum merchant complaints were retrievable this turn (search budget exhausted). Unknown what share of merchant bot traffic is agents vs scrapers; whether Visa TAP / Cloudflare Web Bot Auth adoption will solve identification (Web Bot Auth repo still has open verifier-correctness bugs as of Oct 2026); actual merchant willingness to pay for agent-specific attribution
technical_unlock: HTTP Message Signatures for bots (Cloudflare Web Bot Auth, IETF draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01) and Visa TAP give a verifiable agent identity header; a lightweight verifier/middleware plus analytics that classifies signed-agent vs unsigned-bot vs human and ties sessions to orders is buildable by a solo dev (Next.js middleware, Playwright-based testing of agent flows)
why_now: Agent referral traffic became measurable in 2025-26 (Adobe +393%); OpenAI/Stripe ACP (Sept 2025), Google AP2, Visa TAP all launched; OpenAI pulled back in-chat checkout March 2026, pushing checkout back to merchant sites where merchants must handle agents themselves
existing_solutions: Cloudflare bot management and Web Bot Auth, Visa Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay, Anubis (open source), Shopify agentic storefront tooling, Adobe/Salesforce analytics; none ties signed-agent identity to order attribution for small merchants

domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: Agent retries double-charge customers because idempotency and spend policy live below the orchestration layer
affected_user: Developers shipping payment-capable agents on Stripe/ACP/AP2, and the merchants and end customers who eat duplicate charges and refunds
job_to_be_done: Let an agent create a charge or checkout exactly once per user intent, within a budget, even when timeouts and orchestrator retries happen
current_process: Stripe SDK auto-generates an idempotency key per call; agent frameworks (LangChain, CrewAI) retry the whole tool invocation on timeout with a fresh key; spend caps are configured per toolkit and are not enforced by a neutral party
what_fails: A timeout before confirmation makes the agent re-invoke the tool as a new session, producing two charges (Stripe agent-toolkit issue #402, 49 comments, no maintainer reply). A toolkit release silently ignored a removed actions policy, fail-opening tools (#508). AP2 verifiers never consumed an accepted Payment Mandate, so one user consent could be redeemed for multiple payments; budget caps truncated floats and applied max*100 to all currencies. ACP's MCP binding made the mandatory Idempotency-Key optional for mutating checkout tools
failure_frequency: Unknown per merchant; one commenter observed duplicate effects 32-37 seconds apart against a 30-second caller timeout, i.e. every slow charge is a candidate
cost_of_failure: Unknown in aggregate; each duplicate produces a refund or a chargeback (chargeback fees are borne by the merchant per ACP issue #303). Stripe's dispute fee is not cited in sources, so left unquantified
existing_workaround: Hand-rolled durable pending-claim tables keyed on canonicalized tool arguments (RFC 8785), reconciliation against Stripe object state after ambiguous outcomes, third-party guard projects (SafeAgent, Nobulex, Metrecept signed receipts, paid) promoted in the thread
who_pays_today: Developers' time; merchants via refunds and dispute fees; early paid receipt/attestation services

sources.note: Developer reproduces duplicate charges from agent-level retries; 49 comments through Oct 8, 2026; no Stripe maintainer response visible
v0.7.x silently ignores removed configuration.actions policy, fail-opening the toolset
Developer asks for a third-party spend/policy check before Stripe MCP tools execute
AP2 bug: verifiers never consume an accepted closed Payment Mandate, one consent redeemable for multiple payments; budget cap unit and float-truncation bugs (Sep-Oct 2026)
ACP MCP binding makes mandatory Idempotency-Key optional for mutating checkout tools
Developers still need spending limits and allowlists; they are not built into x402 implementations

firsthand_evidence: A developer building a LangChain/CrewAI agent with Stripe's toolkit reported (May 3, 2026) that a timeout before confirmation caused the agent to retry create_payment_intent as a new invocation with a new auto-generated idempotency key, producing two charges; he says the SDK's network-level retry is fine and the gap is orchestration-level retries above the tool layer. Another commenter measured duplicate effects 32-37 seconds apart against a 30-second timeout.
key_unknowns: How often this hits production merchants vs. hobby projects; whether Stripe's open PR #419 resolves it; whether merchants would pay for an independent pre-action claim/receipt service versus building it in-house; several thread participants are vendors or self-disclosed AI agents, inflating apparent demand
technical_unlock: Deterministic action IDs from canonicalized tool intent (RFC 8785 JCS) plus a durable claim/receipt ledger that any framework can call before money moves; MCP makes it practical to insert such a guard as a proxy tool server in front of Stripe/ACP tools
why_now: Stripe agent toolkit, ACP (Sept 2025), AP2 and x402 all shipped within 12 months; agent frameworks retry by default; first production duplicate-charge reports appeared in 2026
existing_solutions: Stripe idempotency keys (SDK level only), AP2 mandates with budget constraints (buggy per issues), SafeAgent, Nobulex, Metrecept (signed receipts, paid), argentum-core; no widely adopted neutral guard

domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: No dispute process or durable evidence for agent-initiated transactions that go wrong without being fraud
affected_user: Merchants, PSPs and agent platforms handling disputes where an agent bought within/outside its mandate; card issuers; end users whose agent mis-bought
job_to_be_done: Resolve 'the agent bought the wrong thing / exceeded its mandate / merchant did not perform' and prove at dispute time (up to 5-7 years later) what the user actually authorized
current_process: Card-network chargebacks designed for human buyers; AP2 and ACP produce mandates and receipts but ACP's 'dispute' adjustment type has no process behind it and AP2 only says its audit trail 'aids' dispute resolution; merchants keep SD-JWTs with no defined retention or key-recovery method
what_fails: Liability 'remains largely unresolved once a dispute moves past straightforward fraud' (Worldpay, quoted in ACP #303); Amex agent protection covers only the cardholder; merchants absorb chargeback fees for agent-caused errors; agent platforms have no forum to present mandates; small-value disputes are not worth contesting; ES256 mandates cannot be re-verified years later because JWKS endpoints vanish, keys rotate, issuers disappear
failure_frequency: Unknown; dispute windows cited: 120 days (card), 2 years (Reg E), 5 years (BSA)
cost_of_failure: Unknown; merchants bear chargeback fees and lost goods; specific figures not found
existing_workaround: Keep checkout on the merchant's own site so existing chargeback rules apply; treat agent purchases like cardholder purchases; community-authored evidence pack formats (AP2 #338 reference pack v1.2-1.6) and a proposed ACP dispute extension (ATDRP, SEP #303) still awaiting a sponsor as of Oct 19, 2026
who_pays_today: Merchants (chargeback fees, lost disputes), PSPs (dispute operations), card networks (rule-making), developers writing their own evidence stores

sources.note: SEP proposing a dispute-resolution extension; cites Worldpay on unresolved liability and lists non-fraud dispute cases ACP/AP2 do not handle; seeking OpenAI/Stripe sponsor Oct 19, 2026
34-comment thread: spec leaves retention/retrieval of mandate evidence undefined; keys cannot be re-verified over 5-7 year dispute windows; retention_profile proposed
Open issue: no revocation path for open mandates (standing agent authority cannot be rescinded)
PSP commentary on why OpenAI retreated from in-chat checkout

firsthand_evidence: The author of AP2 issue #338 (Aug 21, 2026) wrote that the spec tells implementers to keep SD-JWTs and disclosures but says nothing about retrieval or retention, that dispute windows run five to seven years, and that an ES256 mandate can only be re-verified if the verifier can still obtain key material valid at transaction time, which JWKS rotation and issuer disappearance make impossible. The ACP #303 author listed cases (merchant non-performance, charge exceeding mandate, mandate reuse after expiry, cart not matching instruction) and said merchants absorb losses through chargeback fees while agent platforms have no forum to present mandates.
key_unknowns: Actual volume of agent-initiated disputes today is tiny (OpenAI reported 8% of aware users had used Instant Checkout); whether card networks will set liability rules themselves (Visa/Mastercard programs) before a third party can; several thread participants self-disclosed as AI agents, so apparent community demand is partly synthetic
technical_unlock: Signed mandate + receipt chains (AP2/ACP) create machine-verifiable evidence for the first time; an offline-verifiable evidence pack with RFC 3161 timestamps and key snapshots is a well-specified, small piece of software
why_now: AP2 (Sept 2025) and ACP introduced cryptographic mandates; first non-fraud agent disputes are appearing in 2026; networks have not published agent-scope dispute rules
existing_solutions: Card-network chargebacks; Amex cardholder-only agent protection; AP2 reference evidence pack (community); ATDRP SEP #303 (unsponsored); PSP dispute tooling (Chargeflow, Stripe Radar) not agent-aware

domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: API and data sellers adopting machine-payment rails (x402) get probed but not paid, and payments are not bound to delivered work
affected_user: Developers selling APIs/data to agents via x402 or similar pay-per-request rails; agent builders who must fund and authorize wallets
job_to_be_done: Charge an autonomous agent a few cents per call and reliably receive payment for work actually delivered
current_process: HTTP 402 challenge, agent signs a stablecoin payment, a facilitator broadcasts it on-chain, server then returns the response; wallet approval gates sit in front of agent spending
what_fails: Facilitators broadcast payments without verifying execution, producing 'paid-but-denied' and 'unpaid-service' outcomes (five practical low-cost attacks identified); agents probe endpoints but rarely pay because they lack funded wallets or sessions; when a human must approve each micropayment the economics collapse; TRM Labs found only a fraction of x402 volume is attributable to AI agents (scripts and self-dealing look identical); adjusted volume fell ~77% from a Nov 2025 peak of $5.15M to $1.19M by May 2026
failure_frequency: Per production report, most agent probes never convert; volume figures above (Artemis via CryptoSlate; contested by a Dune dashboard showing ~130M all-time transactions)
cost_of_failure: Unknown; lost revenue for sellers, unpaid compute, and security exposure
existing_workaround: API keys and prepaid credits instead of per-call payment; allowlists and hand-built spending limits; MPP (Stripe) alongside x402
who_pays_today: Coinbase/Cloudflare (facilitators), developers' time, API sellers eating unpaid calls

sources.note: Five practical attacks on x402 leading to unpaid-service or paid-but-denied

firsthand_evidence: A developer running both x402 and MPP in production wrote that agents probe the paid endpoints but rarely convert, because converting a probe to a payment requires agents with funded sessions or wallets; he says the bottleneck is not UX or pricing. Academic analyses add that facilitators settle without checking the service was performed.
key_unknowns: Whether genuine agent demand for pay-per-call exists at all (CoinDesk: 'demand is just not there yet'); which side (seller or agent) would pay for execution-bound escrow; headline x402 volumes are disputed across TRM/Artemis/Dune
technical_unlock: Escrow-style execution binding (A402 proposal) and signed receipts; MCP servers can wrap x402 so agents carry budgets; stablecoin settlement is cheap enough that per-call escrow is feasible
why_now: x402 launched by Coinbase in 2025 with Cloudflare support; Stripe MPP in 2026; first security papers and production conversion data appeared in 2026
existing_solutions: Coinbase x402 and facilitator, Cloudflare pay-per-crawl (x402-compatible), Stripe MPP, A402 (academic), Skyfire, Nevermined

domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: Small site operators pay AI-crawler bandwidth while licensing/compensation schemes reach only large or Cloudflare-fronted publishers
affected_user: Self-hosted and small-publisher site operators (code forges, hobby sites, regional publishers), independent creators
job_to_be_done: Stop or get paid for AI crawling without blocking real users or paying for the crawlers' bandwidth
current_process: robots.txt blocklists (ai.robots.txt), proof-of-work gates (Anubis), Cloudflare's default block on ad pages from Sept 15, 2026 and Pay Per Crawl, now shifting to 'Pay Per Use' with two launch partners (Ceramic.ai, You.com)
what_fails: Crawlers use residential proxies and headless browsers that pass challenges; new unidentified bots (e.g. 'nbot', 26,772 hits and 2.4 GB on one small site in July 2026) appear faster than blocklists update; pay-per-crawl only applies to sites routed through Cloudflare and one analysis estimates it yields tens to low hundreds of dollars a month at a million page views; Cloudflare itself says negotiated deals do not scale beyond the largest publishers; the RSL standard's public repo shows almost no activity (one open issue since Sept 2025)
failure_frequency: Continuous for exposed hosts; no aggregate statistic found this turn
cost_of_failure: Bandwidth and CPU (one firsthand report: 2.4 GB/month from a single bot on a small site); operator time; false positives blocking legitimate users (Anubis issues on Git clone and Internet Archive crawler)
existing_workaround: Password-gating public repos, stacking Anubis plus auth, moving behind Cloudflare, or giving up and tolerating the load
who_pays_today: Site operators (hosting bills, time); Cloudflare (building the market); large publishers via negotiated licensing deals

domain: NEW MARKET STRUCTURES ENABLED BY AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS
title: Prediction-market traders face settlement failures and resolution errors with no independent monitoring or recourse
affected_user: Active and algorithmic traders on Polymarket and Kalshi; researchers using these markets as data
job_to_be_done: Know that matched orders will settle, that markets resolve per their rules, and get recourse when they do not
current_process: Polymarket: UMA optimistic oracle, proposed result stands after 2 hours unless disputed, token-holder vote; Kalshi: internal team plus Outcome Review Committee; traders report problems via GitHub issues and Discord
what_fails: After Polymarket's April 28, 2026 CLOB V2 cutover a trader measured ~35% of matched market BUYs reverting on-chain settlement, skewed toward would-be winners (48% vs 15%); three others confirmed, no maintainer reply, and the client repo was archived May 25, 2026. Matched GTC maker orders delivered no CTF tokens ~50% of the time (#328). WSJ-reported analysis: >60% of active UMA voters linkable to Polymarket accounts; >50% of votes in top-10 wallets in most disputes; Polymarket said it could not refund after a $7M market swing. Polymarket changed short-dated crypto resolution to TWAP only after months of complaints and a study finding a five-second exploit draining millions. Kalshi mis-graded multiple NFL win-total markets in Jan 2026 with Discord as the only recourse; a $54M class action followed a death-exception ruling in March 2026
failure_frequency: Settlement reverts ~35% of market buys for one trader over the post-cutover window (May 2026); resolution disputes recur monthly across both venues per coverage
cost_of_failure: Millions drained via the crypto-resolution exploit (CoinDesk); $7M market swing with no refunds; individual trader reported net -$39.82 on settled trades while winners failed to settle
existing_workaround: Pause live trading until a post-mortem appears; complain on Discord; file CFTC complaints; class actions; build private settlement monitors
who_pays_today: Traders (losses, time), platforms (legal), the founder's own paper-trading tool addresses strategy testing but not settlement/resolution risk

existing_solutions: Polymarket's own docs and Discord, Kalshi Outcome Review Committee, Alphascope and similar commentary blogs, Dune dashboards; no independent settlement-failure or dispute-tracking service found

title: Businesses deploying AI agents are losing insurance coverage for agent errors faster than replacement products appear
affected_user: SMBs and mid-market companies deploying agents in customer-facing or financial workflows; their brokers
job_to_be_done: Transfer the risk of an agent's erroneous action (wrong purchase, bad advice, data damage) to an insurer at a known price
current_process: Rely on 'silent' coverage under cyber, Tech E&O, CGL and D&O; brokers try to place specialty AI liability (AIUC, Armilla, Testudo, HSB SMB product, Apollo/ibott)
what_fails: ISO generative-AI exclusion endorsements began attaching to CGL renewals from January 2026; one source counts 60+ P&C groups filing AI exclusions by July 2026 (AIG, WR Berkley, Great American, Berkshire Hathaway, Chubb named); standard E&O assumes a human professional made the decision, leaving hallucination liability and multi-step autonomous error chains uncovered; specialty policies are expensive, limited, often tied to audits; dedicated AI liability market estimated at only ~$130M globally in 2026 because insurers lack loss data
failure_frequency: Every renewal cycle from 2026 onward for CGL; unknown claim frequency
cost_of_failure: Unknown; uninsured losses fall on the deploying business; no primary claim statistics found
existing_workaround: Keep humans in the loop for money-moving actions, contractual indemnities with vendors, self-insure, or avoid deployment
who_pays_today: Businesses (premiums for limited products, uninsured losses), brokers (placement time), insurers/MGAs building products (AIUC, Armilla)

cost_of_failure: Weeks of lost income per worker (Amazon Flex 3-4 week peak appeals); Grubhub paid $622.85 penalties plus $622.85 fines in one Seattle case; HRW describes workers left without income
existing_workaround: Multi-apping to hedge, Discord/Reddit crowdsourced appeal templates, small-claims suits, law-firm demand letters, FareShare lost-wage calculator for organizers
who_pays_today: Workers (lost income), city labor offices (Seattle OLS enforcement), law firms on contingency, unions and worker centers
